Chapter 7: Questioning Beliefs and the Power of Doubt.
At the heart of awareness, there’s something powerful—a willingness to question what you think you know. Most of us live inside this web of beliefs. They’re about ourselves, about others, and about the world. And honestly, they can feel so solid, so unshakeable, that we rarely even notice they’re there. But here’s the thing: these beliefs shape every perception, every reaction, and every decision we make.
What if some of those beliefs just aren’t true? What if they’re nothing more than stories we picked up—maybe from our families, our culture, or just experiences along the way?
Sooner or later, most people run into a moment when one of those long-held beliefs gets challenged. Maybe it’s the idea that success means you have to work harder than everyone else. Or that love is always something you have to earn. Then life throws a curveball—and suddenly, the old story just doesn’t fit. That’s when discomfort creeps in. Some people double down, clinging even tighter to what they’ve always believed. Others start to wonder, “Is this really true?”
Think about a young professional who’s grown up believing that vulnerability equals weakness. At work, this might mean hiding any mistake, never asking for help, and always putting on a brave face—even when things are falling apart. Eventually, the pressure gets overwhelming, and burnout kicks in. Then, one day, in a moment of exhaustion, they open up to a colleague. Instead of judgment, they get understanding and support. And just like that, the old belief starts to wobble. Maybe vulnerability isn’t weakness after all.
It’s funny—doubt gets such a bad rap. Most people see it as a problem, but it can actually be a powerful ally. It’s like a little crack in the wall that lets the light in. When you start to question your beliefs, you make space for something new.
Sure, it can feel scary. Uncertainty usually does. But that’s exactly where real growth happens. Being willing to say, “I don’t know,” is actually the beginning of wisdom.
Now, this isn’t about tossing out every belief you have. It’s more about holding them lightly—just noticing which stories bring you peace, and which ones bring pain. When a belief causes suffering, it’s worth asking yourself, “Is this really true? Who would I be without this story?” Sometimes just asking the question is enough to loosen its grip.
Picture a parent who believes that good parenting means always putting their child’s needs first. Over time, resentment and exhaustion start to build. But when they question that belief, something shifts. They realize that self-care isn’t selfish—it’s essential. And suddenly, the relationship with their child becomes more balanced, more joyful.
Most people never take the time to really examine the stories they’re living by. But when you do, something amazing happens. Life opens up. You find more flexibility, more creativity, and a whole lot more freedom.
That’s the real power of doubt. It’s not about tearing everything down—it’s about making room for what’s real, and what’s true.
